title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers have deployed AI tools to impersonate trusted figures, including cloning the voice of a South Florida immigration attorney to solicit payments from immigrants. The system here is social engineering amplified by deepfakes, deepening a class of fraud that predates AI but now executes with greater fidelity. Detection would have required victims to verify requests through independent contact channels rather than relying on voice or video alone.

The failure is one of access to generative tools without friction or verification. Deepfake technology and voice-cloning software became cheap and easy enough that criminals could deploy them against specific targets. No gating mechanism, authentication layer, or human review stood between the scammer and their victim.

Whether these specific cases represent a novel threat or simply a more convincing execution of longstanding scams is not established. What is clear is that AI made the fraud more persuasive, and persuasiveness is the scammer's only tool.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit fraud across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report found that Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Criminals use deepfake technology to clone voices, create fake photos, and spoof phone numbers to impersonate trusted individuals. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice was cloned to target immigrants and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints totaling nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints with over $10.4 million in losses.

Authorities say AI is making common scams like the grandparent scam, romance schemes, and emergency requests far more convincing. Banks warn customers that fraudsters are creating increasingly believable impersonation attempts. To protect themselves, people should establish code words with family members to verify identity, verify urgent requests by contacting the person through known phone numbers, avoid sending money based solely on phone calls, and report suspected scams to law enforcement. As AI tools become cheaper and more accessible, experts say verification rather than speed represents consumers' strongest defense against these emerging threats.
